seeds.question: What does TERI do?
seeds.answer:
TERI is an independent, not-for-profit research institute focused on advancing a cleaner, more sustainable planet. Its work spans climate and air quality, energy, agriculture, biotechnology, infrastructure, natural resources and social transformation, and it aims to turn research into practical solutions and policy advice. [1]

### Research and technical solutions
- TERI conducts research on renewable energy, climate change, air quality, sustainable agriculture, industrial biotechnology, green shipping, infrastructure, and waste, water and natural resources. [1]
- Its work includes developing technology products and technical services, as well as designing and rating buildings for their carbon footprint and resource efficiency. [1]
- TERI has also developed and implemented projects on sustainable and energy-efficient building design and technologies. [2]

### Policy and public engagement
- TERI provides policy research and advice to government and corporate bodies on issues including climate change, energy and air pollution, and has contributed to national policy work and India’s international negotiating positions. [1]
- It works with young people to co-create evidence-based learning intended to encourage environmentally conscious behaviour and help them address climate change. [1]
- Its resource-efficiency work has included policy research and consultancy on economic sectors, natural-resource trade and the governance of resource revenues. [1]

### Programmes and initiatives
- Through Lighting a Billion Lives, TERI worked to improve access to clean lighting; the 2024 brochure reports that the initiative reached nearly 4.5 million people across 24 Indian states and 12 countries in South Asia and Africa. [1]
- Its SMILE programme promotes renewable energy and energy-efficient technologies in micro-enterprise clusters to improve productivity and entrepreneurs’ incomes. [1]
- TERI’s National Centre of Excellence on Green Ports and Shipping, constituted in 2022 with the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, works on policy and regulation, alternative technologies and project reports to support decarbonisation and a circular economy in shipping. [1]

### Reach and scale
- The 2024 brochure says TERI had more than 700 professionals and regional centres and campuses in Gurugram, Bengaluru, Guwahati, Mumbai, Panaji and Nainital. [1]
- The brochure reports research and outreach activities in over 40 countries. [1]
- TERI was established in 1974; research in energy, environment and sustainable development began toward the end of 1982. [1][2]

seeds.question: What research does TERI do?
seeds.answer:
TERI conducts multidisciplinary, action-oriented research across energy, environment, climate change and sustainable development, with work spanning areas such as renewable energy, agriculture, urban development, mobility and natural-resource management [1][2][7]. It combines research and policy analysis with technology development, field implementation and engagement with governments, businesses and communities [2][5][7].

### Research areas
- TERI researches clean and renewable energy, energy efficiency, advanced biofuels and decentralized energy solutions [1][5][6].
- Its work includes climate change, air pollution, sustainable agriculture, biotechnology, forestry, biodiversity, water security and land-resource management [1][2][3][6].
- It studies sustainable cities and infrastructure, including green buildings, transport and mobility, sanitation, sewage, solid waste and air quality [2][3][7].
- Research also addresses resource efficiency and the use of materials, including iron and cement [2][3][4].

### From research to solutions
- TERI develops and tests solutions from laboratory to pilot and field scale, and works to validate business models early [3].
- Its research supports technologies and practical interventions, including renewable-energy solutions, bio-based agricultural inputs, green-building design and resource-efficient practices [1][2][3][6].
- The institute provides policy advice and consultancy, and has contributed research and inputs to policy development and implementation [3][5][6][7].

### Methods and collaboration
- TERI describes its approach as interdisciplinary and integrated, using evidence- and data-based decision-making [3].
- Its work includes education and outreach, capacity building and support for stakeholders, alongside partnerships nationally and internationally [2][3].
- It collaborates with governments, businesses, civil society, industry and international organizations [2][7].

### Historical development
- TERI was established in 1974; an older account says research in energy, environment and sustainable development began toward the end of 1982 [1][8].
- The 2024–25 annual-report edition describes more than 50 years of multidisciplinary research, policy advocacy and development of policies and technologies [5].

seeds.question: What is clean energy?
seeds.answer:
Clean energy is energy produced or used through approaches that emphasize renewable sources and efficiency while limiting environmental harm. TERI’s work includes renewable-energy technologies and energy-efficient solutions, while other statements in the sources connect clean energy with lower greenhouse-gas emissions and access to reliable, affordable power [1][3][6].

### Technologies and approaches
- TERI identifies industrial energy efficiency, renewable-energy technologies, electricity and fuels, and energy assessment and modelling as areas of its clean-energy work [1].
- Examples discussed include solar and wind power, green hydrogen, biofuels, biogas, and carbon capture and reuse [1][2][7].

### Goals
- Clean-energy efforts are linked to reducing greenhouse-gas emissions and supporting climate resilience [7].
- India’s energy priorities have included access to clean, reliable and affordable energy, alongside expanding power access [6][3].

### Cooperation and implementation
- TERI says its work focuses on developing and encouraging adoption of clean-energy technologies, integrating renewables into the grid, and improving efficiency in industries and public utilities [1].
- The 2015 U.S.-India summit highlighted renewable-energy expansion, improved efficiency, clean-energy finance, and cooperation on grid integration [3][7].

seeds.question: What are green buildings?
seeds.answer:
Green buildings are designed, constructed and operated to use energy, water and other natural resources efficiently, reduce environmental impacts and waste, and provide a healthier, more comfortable indoor environment. Their sustainability depends on a whole-life approach, from planning and design through construction and operation [5][9].

### Design and performance
- Sustainable features can include efficient water and energy use, renewable energy, recycled or recyclable materials, effective landscaping and building-management systems, and improved indoor air quality [9].
- Climate-responsive design, building orientation, efficient materials and systems, and renewable energy can improve performance; for example, solar-passive design can reduce reliance on conventional heating, cooling, ventilation and lighting [7][8].
- Planning for sustainability at the initial design stage helps account for the supply chain, resource reuse, civic amenities and waste disposal [9].

### Ratings and assessment
- Green ratings assess a building’s predicted environmental performance over its life cycle, using benchmarks for matters such as energy and water use, renewable energy and occupant comfort [5].
- GRIHA is a rating tool for assessing buildings and habitats against nationally accepted benchmarks. Its variants include SVAGRIHA for smaller buildings and GRIHA LD for large developments [4][6].
- Rating systems can support measured improvement and help validate sustainability claims; the benefits of incentives, such as tax breaks or development-charge discounts, depend on the schemes offered by relevant institutions [4][5].

### Benefits and challenges
- One source gives potential benefits including 30–50% lower energy consumption, up to 40% lower freshwater demand, and 30–40% lower operating costs [5].
- Green building approaches can also help protect biodiversity, reduce pollution and waste, and improve occupant health, comfort and productivity [5][7].
- Challenges described include higher construction costs in some cases, difficulty sourcing materials and services, restrictive building rules and codes, and financing hurdles [7][9].

### Examples of performance
- At Suzlon One Earth, renewable energy and integrated design were associated with a reported 47.2% reduction in energy consumption against GRIHA benchmarks; the campus achieved a 5-star GRIHA rating [7].
- IIT Kanpur’s building used solar-passive techniques and an earth-air tunnel, with reported reductions of 47% in energy consumption and 65% in water consumption against GRIHA benchmarks [7].
- Royal Orange County in Pune incorporates solar power, sewage treatment and rainwater harvesting, and was described as targeting a 5-star GRIHA rating [4].

### TERI’s work
- TERI’s buildings work combines research, policy advocacy and on-ground implementation, and includes environmental design consultancy, energy and resource-efficiency audits, and project management [1].
- It also undertakes water audits and provides technical assistance toward GRIHA Water Positive Certification [3].

seeds.question: Tell about the director general of TERI
seeds.answer:
**Dr Vibha Dhawan is TERI’s Director General** [1][2].

### Leadership and research
- Her association with TERI dates to 1985. She led TERI School of Advanced Studies as Vice-Chancellor from 2005 to 2007 [1].
- Her recent research interests include biofuels. She has authored six books and more than 50 publications [1].
- Under her leadership, TERI established the National Centre of Excellence in Green Port & Shipping in collaboration with India’s Ministry of Ports, Shipping, and Waterways [1].
- She was instrumental in establishing TERI’s Micropropagation Technology Park and developed biotechnology postgraduate e-content for the University Grants Commission [1].

### Appointments and contributions
- She is a Fellow of the National Academy of Sciences, India, and an Adjunct Professor at Consul General South Asia Partnership, Michigan State University [1].
- She is a task force member of national committees with the Department of Biotechnology, the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council, and the Biotech Consortium India; she also serves on the Networks Strategy Council advising the Sustainable Development Solutions Network [1].
- Her earlier roles include Co-ordinator for the Asia Pacific Consortium on Agriculture Biotechnology, Advisor to the Director General of CIMMYT, and Deputy Director of Research Partnerships & Co-ordination with the Borlaug Institute for South Asia [1].
- She has served on the boards of Jawahar Lal Nehru University, Ambedkar University, Ayurvet Foundation, and the Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International [1].

seeds.question: What is the mission and vision of TERI?
seeds.answer:
TERI’s mission is to support the transition to a cleaner, sustainable future through conserving and using energy and other resources efficiently, and through innovative ways to minimize and reuse waste [2]. Its forward-looking vision for 2025–30 emphasizes scaling sustainable solutions toward a net-zero, resource-efficient and inclusive development trajectory [4].

### Mission and goals
- TERI pursues its mission by seeking wider access to clean energy, a global transition to renewable energy, greater energy efficiency, and more efficient use of materials, especially iron and cement [2].
- Its goals also include conserving and improving access to water; enabling environmentally sustainable cities; building climate resilience; reducing pollution; enhancing ecosystem services; developing green mobility; and supporting sustainable food production and nutritional security [3].

### Vision for 2025–30
- In the short term, TERI’s strategic focus is on piloting innovative technologies, advancing regulatory frameworks, building capacity and fostering community-centred sustainable practices across areas including clean energy, agriculture, water and waste management, and climate resilience [4].
- In the longer term, it envisions scaling interventions through research, wider deployment of clean technologies, integrated sustainability frameworks and stronger international partnerships, while advancing decarbonization, circular-economy solutions and climate-smart infrastructure [4].

seeds.question: Can you provide a brief history of The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI)?
seeds.answer:
TERI was established in 1974 as the Tata Energy Research Institute, with Shri JRD Tata as its first Chairman. Its early leadership included Shri Darbari Seth and Dr R K Pachauri, whose long tenure as its first Director helped shape the institute’s development and public profile [2].

### Founding and early leadership
- Shri Darbari Seth became Vice-Chairman of TERI’s Governing Council in 1975; both he and JRD Tata were devoted to sustainable energy use and environmental stewardship [2].
- Dr R K Pachauri became TERI’s first Director in 1981 and served in that role until 2015, later serving as Executive Vice-Chairman until 2017 [2].
- Seth was a builder of Tata Chemicals and, at one stage, chaired 14 companies; his contribution to TERI was part of a wider engagement with sustainability [1][2].

### Growth and recognition
- During Pachauri’s leadership and global advocacy, TERI became a leading voice on energy and climate policy [2].
- TERI’s work has included multidisciplinary research, policy engagement, capacity building, technology development and on-the-ground implementation [8].
- Pachauri was elected Chair of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change in 2002 and received the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize on the IPCC’s behalf, jointly with Al Gore [1].

### Research and mission
- TERI describes its work as advancing solutions in energy, environment, climate change and sustainable development, including clean energy, sustainable agriculture, water security, land management, air pollution and low-emission transport [2].
- Its stated mission is to support transitions to a cleaner, sustainable future through conserving and efficiently using energy and other resources, and minimizing and reusing waste [3].

seeds.question: What are the environmental impacts of solar energy?
seeds.answer:
Solar energy can reduce emissions and pollution, but its environmental effects depend on how projects are sited, built and operated. Large solar plants can affect land, water and ecosystems, while solar irrigation can bring agricultural and emissions benefits but may add pressure to water resources depending on where and how it is used [4][5].

### Land and ecosystems
- Large solar projects can take productive farmland, restrict access to common resources such as pastoral land, and displace buildings or affect the livelihoods of landowners, tenants and landless workers [4].
- Potential ecological effects include soil erosion, water scarcity, loss of tree cover and natural habitat, and reduced soil moisture-holding capacity following the loss of organic matter [4].
- Land-use conflicts can be reduced by carefully considering prior land use, wildlife corridors, habitats, biodiversity hotspots and community use of common land when selecting sites [1].

### Water and solar irrigation
- Solar irrigation may improve agricultural productivity and incomes by increasing yields, expanding cropped areas, enabling higher-value crops or multiple cropping, and lowering recurring pumping costs [5].
- Solar pumps can reduce emissions when they replace grid- or diesel-powered pumps, but increased solar irrigation could place additional pressure on water resources depending on implementation [5].
- Water-efficient technologies for cleaning solar panels are recommended, particularly because many plants are in water-stressed regions [1].

### Materials and waste
- Photovoltaic panels contain materials such as polymers and lead and cadmium compounds that require treatment before disposal to avoid environmental and health impacts [4].
- In the 2021 report, solar waste was described as being incinerated or landfilled in the absence of a policy to manage it; the report estimated that PV-panel waste could reach 200,000 tonnes by 2030 and around 1.8 million tonnes by 2050 [4].
- The report recommends a comprehensive mechanism for using environmentally sustainable materials in module manufacturing and processing end-of-life module waste [1].

seeds.question: How does climate change affect water availability in India?
seeds.answer:
Climate change makes water availability in India more variable and less predictable, affecting rainfall, river flows, groundwater, and water security. Its effects differ across regions, and include both greater water stress and more damaging floods [3][6].

### Changing rainfall and water supply
- Erratic monsoons and heavier rainfall events can be followed by longer dry spells, increasing the risk of both floods and droughts; the overall change in water availability was described as unknown in a 2019 study, while increased variability was identified as certain [6][8].
- A study cited in the water-resilience paper found that June–September rainfall declined by about 6% over 1951–2015, while daily precipitation extremes exceeding 150 mm increased by about 75% over central India [6].
- Climate change can reduce groundwater recharge through changing precipitation patterns, while droughts and higher temperatures contribute to falling groundwater levels and water scarcity [6][7].

### Rivers, glaciers, and regional risks
- Himalayan glacial melt affects the hydrological cycle and river flows; as glaciers retreat, meltwater feeding northern Indian rivers is expected to decrease over the long term, with consequences for downstream agriculture and other water users [6].
- In Uttarakhand, changes in the hydrological cycle are already affecting water availability for agriculture and causing crop-water stress in several districts; the cited assessment identifies Pauri Garhwal and Dehradun as especially vulnerable to reduced water availability [5].
- Coastal areas face sea-level-rise risks, while other regions face erratic rainfall and drought; climate-resilient water management is therefore needed to address differing regional challenges [3][6].

### Consequences for people and water management
- Floods and droughts threaten water resources, and floods can damage infrastructure, displace people, and contaminate water sources; droughts can worsen water scarcity and harm crops and livestock [6].
- Changes in river flows can affect irrigation and food security, while water stress can threaten livelihoods that depend on agriculture [4][5][7].
- Recommended responses include integrated water-resources management, better climate and water monitoring, stronger coordination among institutions, and community involvement in decision-making [3].

seeds.question: What approaches reduce air pollution in Indian cities?
seeds.answer:
Approaches to reducing air pollution in Indian cities combine coordinated regional and city-level planning with measures targeting transport, industry, waste, homes, and dust. They include both emissions controls and the monitoring, public engagement, and infrastructure needed to put those controls into effect [2][3][5][6].

### Planning and monitoring
- Use emission inventories, air-quality monitoring and modelling, and source-apportionment studies to identify pollution sources and assess control options [1][3][5].
- Coordinate action across sectors and across city and state boundaries, since pollution can travel beyond the place where it is emitted [5][6].
- Prepare city-specific clean-air and emergency action plans, and use regional plans alongside them; a 2023 study recommended this approach for Patna, Indore, and Dewas [1][5].

### Transport
- Expand public transport and make walking and cycling safer and more accessible; the recommendations also include managing congestion and considering congestion pricing [2][3][5].
- Reduce vehicle emissions through cleaner fuels and vehicles, electric vehicles, stricter standards, and phasing out older vehicles. A 2023 plan proposed scrapping older private and commercial vehicles and expanding electric two-wheelers and buses [3][4][5].
- Improve traffic flow and control road dust through measures such as mechanized sweeping and roadside planting [5].

### Industry, energy, homes, and waste
- Tighten industrial and power-plant emissions controls, improve monitoring, and apply measures such as zig-zag technology in brick kilns [1][3].
- Promote cleaner cooking fuels and electric or induction cooking, and reduce open burning of waste and crop residues through better waste collection, composting, and residue management [1][2][3][4][5].
- Control dust from construction with site coverings and other dust-reduction measures [1][5].

### Public engagement and implementation
- Raise public awareness about pollution sources and health effects, and involve communities in air-quality management [1][2][5].
- Support implementation with adequate infrastructure and coordinated policy; financial constraints, limited technical capacity, data gaps, and weak public participation are identified as obstacles [2][3].

seeds.question: Why does sustainable agriculture matter for smallholder farmers?
seeds.answer:
Sustainable agriculture matters for smallholder farmers because it seeks to sustain food production while protecting the natural resources and ecosystems agriculture depends on, and to support farmers’ livelihoods and resilience. Its importance is especially clear in India, where a 2023 blueprint says about 86% of farmers are small and marginal, and stresses that sustainable practices need to be economically viable for farmers, not only environmentally beneficial [5][6].

### Livelihoods and farm viability
- Fragmented, small landholdings can make sustainable practices such as crop diversification difficult; aggregating farmers and supporting community-led adaptation may help address this challenge [3][4].
- Chemical-based farming can be more profitable than organic farming, while limited market access and inadequate prices can weaken farmers’ incentives to adopt sustainable practices [3][4].
- Policies and incentives need to recognize smallholder and tenant farmers, account for differences in farmers’ income and circumstances, and make sure benefits reach farmers themselves [4].

### Resilience and environmental benefits
- Sustainable agriculture can combine improved productivity and livelihoods with resilience, biodiversity conservation, food security and reduced environmental impacts [5].
- Agroforestry, conservation tillage and water-efficient farming are identified as practices that can generate carbon credits; an article dated 2024 describes carbon markets as a potential source of income diversification and climate resilience for small farmers [7].
- Land and agriculture are interconnected with water, soil and wider ecosystems, so sustainable farming also depends on stewardship of shared landscapes and natural resources [3].

### What can support adoption
- Community initiatives, farmer aggregation and stronger access to information and markets are identified as ways to support sustainable farming among smallholders [4].
- The Sustainable Agriculture Division of TERI says its research aims to reduce reliance on synthetic chemical inputs while improving soil health, carbon sequestration, nutrient-use efficiency and crop productivity [1].
- A study of 590 farming households in West Bengal in 2004–05 found negative energy surpluses to be near-universal across land-size groups; it found no evidence that household size explained the negative surplus [8].

seeds.question: How can buildings be made more energy efficient?
seeds.answer:
Buildings can be made more energy efficient through integrated design, efficient building systems and materials, renewable energy, and upgrades to existing buildings. The approach combines reducing energy demand with meeting more of the remaining demand through efficient systems and renewable sources [1][3].

### Design and building systems
- Use passive solar design, appropriate building orientation and shading, daylighting, and suitable windows to reduce heating, cooling and lighting needs; the right choices depend on the climate and the building’s use [3][4].
- Design efficient lighting and heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems, with suitable controls and operating strategies [3].
- Choose energy-efficient materials and construction methods, and use renewable energy systems such as solar power and hot-water systems to supply part of the building’s energy needs [3].
- For glazed buildings, balance daylight with heat and glare control: the 2013 article gives 20–40% as an optimum glazed area for a typical day-use commercial building and recommends shading, appropriate glass and daylight-linked lighting controls [4].

### Water, waste and renewable energy
- Improve water efficiency, reduce waste and pollution, and use sustainable building materials; the 2014 article says these strategies can reduce building energy consumption by 30–80% [1].
- Examples in that article include treating and reusing wastewater at Govardhan Eco Village, and combining on-site and off-site renewable energy at Suzlon One Earth, which it reports reduced energy consumption by 47.2% against the GRIHA benchmark [1].
- The RETREAT complex described in the 2004 article used passive design, an earth-tunnel cooling system, efficient lighting, solar hot water and wastewater recycling; the article reports annual savings of about 250,000 units of electricity and 2,100 LPG cylinders [3].

### Existing buildings and barriers
- Retrofitting existing buildings with efficient technologies can reduce energy use; a 2025 article says retrofitting can reduce building load by up to 75% [3][6].
- The 2014 article identifies cumbersome permitting, outdated building codes and financing hurdles as obstacles, and describes incentives such as tax credits, grants, fee reductions and technical assistance as ways to encourage green construction and retrofits [1].
- The 2009 article cautions against extensive glass use without attention to climate, orientation and insulation, and advocates an integrated approach involving design, materials, construction, building systems and renewable energy [2].

seeds.question: GRIHA rating for green buildings
seeds.answer:
GRIHA is India’s national green-building rating system, jointly developed by the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy and TERI in 2007; it is administered and promoted by GRIHA Council [1][2]. It evaluates a building’s environmental performance across its life cycle, using qualitative and quantitative criteria, and includes variants for small buildings and large developments [1][5].

### How the rating works
- GRIHA assesses buildings against criteria intended to measure and manage their environmental performance, with ratings based on the criteria a project attempts [1][2].
- The system is designed for different climatic zones and regional variations, and brings together national and state codes and norms into a common set of criteria [2].
- It emphasizes integrated design, cost-effective strategies, energy-loss reduction, and occupants’ acoustic, thermal and visual comfort [2].
- GRIHA is a voluntary rating, distinct from mandatory environmental clearance; its pre-certification process considers environmental-clearance requirements for projects that require them [6].

### Rating variants
- SVAGRIHA is for small homes, offices and commercial buildings under 2,500 square metres of built-up area [5].
- GRIHA LD is for large developments such as campuses, townships and special economic zones [5].
- GRIHA ratings have also been described as awarding buildings between one and five stars according to their score [4].

### What the system seeks to achieve
- The rating aims to reduce resource consumption, waste and buildings’ overall environmental impact, while supporting resource-efficient design, construction, operation and maintenance [4][5].
- Its criteria address energy, environmental, social and health issues; the system also recommends measures such as low-VOC paints, adhesives and sealants to support indoor air quality [2][6].
- In a report published in 2020, GRIHA Council said the rating was then being applied to more than 1,700 projects across India, covering 565 million square feet [2]. The same source reported 85 MWp of renewable-energy installations, annual emissions offsets of 741,801 tCO₂, and annual post-construction energy savings of 2,620,557 MWh associated with rated projects [3].

### Examples and practical support
- A GRIHA-rated UIDAI headquarters in New Delhi achieved a reported 62.2% reduction in energy consumption against the GRIHA benchmark; measures included a 100 kWp solar photovoltaic system and timer-controlled, high-efficacy exterior lighting [3].
- GRIHA Council’s services include performance assessments and documentation support across project stages, as well as assistance with national and international green-building certifications including GRIHA [1].
- A 2014 article described GRIHA pre-certification as support for developers preparing for environmental-clearance review, and stressed that building systems such as rainwater harvesting and sewage treatment require ongoing maintenance [6].

seeds.question: Himalayan Adaptation, Water and Resilience research
seeds.answer:
HI-AWARE (Himalayan Adaptation, Water and Resilience) was a research consortium focused on climate resilience and adaptation in the mountains and floodplains of the Indus, Ganges and Brahmaputra river basins. Its stated goal was to strengthen the resilience and adaptive capacity of poor and vulnerable communities by using research and pilot outcomes to influence policy and practice [1].

### Research scope and aims
- HI-AWARE aimed to generate scientific knowledge about the biophysical, socio-economic, gender-related and governance factors that shape climate vulnerability, and to build evidence about adaptation approaches focused on gender and livelihoods [1].
- Its research addressed water, energy, food security, human health, water-induced hazards and extreme events; it also tested adaptation measures and developed pathways for scaling them up and out [1].
- The consortium’s objectives also included promoting the uptake of adaptation knowledge by decision-makers and citizens, and strengthening interdisciplinary expertise and research and policy networks [1].

### Work and locations
- In the 2014 description, HI-AWARE’s three work packages were Knowledge Generation, Research into Use and Strengthening Expertise. Activities were planned across 12 sites in the Indus, Upper Ganga, Gandaki and Teesta river basins and beyond [1].
- TERI was a consortium partner and, in the 2015–16 reporting period, led HI-AWARE-related research and policy engagement in the Ganga basin in Uttarakhand and the Teesta basin in Sikkim [5]. A 2014 project description also identified TERI as India’s country lead, working in the Upper Ganga and Teesta basins [1].

### Research and adaptation examples
- In the 2015–16 reporting period, work included climate downscaling for selected basins, analysis of climate-related vulnerabilities, research into critical times of year for particular social groups, and glacial research. Workshops in Gangtok and Tehri informed stakeholder mapping and analysis of governance around spring rejuvenation programmes [5].
- A project described in 2023 aimed to develop a Melt Water Vulnerability Index for water-resource management and livelihood resilience in three Indian Himalayan states. It also planned a modelling tool to quantify impacts and adaptation needs, and a policy brief on meltwater vulnerability and local livelihoods [2].
- TERI’s Himalayan research included glacier monitoring and investigation of glacier meltwater’s effects on local communities and livelihoods. Its glacier observatories recorded meteorological and glacier-balance data, while the meltwater project sought to assess communities’ dependence and vulnerability [3][4].

seeds.question: SDG 7 progress on energy access in rural India
seeds.answer:
Rural India’s progress on SDG 7—access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy—has involved expanding electricity access while still facing gaps in reliable supply, clean cooking and the conversion of energy access into livelihoods [4][6][8]. The available figures are mainly from 2011 and describe the scale of the challenge at that time; a later account discusses continuing last-mile challenges but gives no current rural access total [4][6][8].

### Access gaps
- A paper published in 2014 reports that almost 77 million Indian households were without electricity in 2011, and more than 836 million people lacked access to modern cooking fuels [8].
- A workshop account cites Census 2011 figures of about 45% of rural households—75 million households—without electricity, and 86% of rural households relying on traditional biomass for cooking [6].
- The workshop account estimated that providing sustainable, modern and affordable energy to those 75 million households would require about US$75 billion at the costs then stated, and modern cooking methods for rural households about US$5 billion [6].

### What access needs to deliver
- A 2026 account says the next phase of SDG 7 requires clean energy to be reliable, affordable, productive and inclusive, particularly for rural, remote and economically vulnerable communities; it notes unreliable supply, weak distribution infrastructure and limited opportunities to turn access into better livelihoods [4].
- TERI’s Energy Access page describes its work as using sustainable energy to support rural communities’ socio-economic development in a gender-inclusive way, through technological solutions, business models, partnerships and knowledge generation [1].
- The page lists initiatives including village electrification and livelihoods through clean energy, and projects focused on women’s empowerment and decentralised renewable energy [2][3].

### Local and productive-use approaches
- TERI’s Lighting a Billion Lives 2.0 is described as moving beyond basic lighting to using clean energy for micro-enterprises, agriculture and traditional occupations, with the aim of supporting livelihoods and enterprise development [4].
- In the Pokhran pottery cluster, around 150–180 artisan households are being supported with hybrid solar systems; the account says the intervention reduces energy costs by nearly 70% and increases productivity [4].
- A 2014 paper identifies technical, financial, regulatory and institutional barriers to rural energy access, and says successful outcomes require innovation beyond physical access, coordination between energy provision and development, and a structured rural energy-delivery model [8].

reply.question: What did COP negotiators identify as areas to build on for climate finance?
reply.answer:
Climate negotiators and finance discussions identified several ways to strengthen climate finance: improve transparency and predictability, mobilize more public and private funding, and make finance more accessible and balanced between mitigation and adaptation. They also highlighted the need for finance arrangements to reflect developing countries’ needs and equity concerns. [1][2][4][5]

### Negotiating rules and transparency
- An effective Paris Rulebook was seen as important for tracking climate finance clearly and predictably; developing countries called for clear commitments and transparent accounting of financial flows. [1]
- Discussions highlighted the need for shared definitions and robust monitoring and reporting, since inconsistent definitions and disputed accounting can make reported finance difficult to assess. [2][4]
- The 2024 discussions stressed that the New Collective Quantified Goal should address access, scale, timing and transparency, and align with developing countries’ needs and priorities. [4]

### Finance sources and scale
- Negotiators discussed mobilizing finance from public and private sources, including bilateral and multilateral channels, and creating conditions that could encourage private investment in climate action. [1][4][5]
- The 2024 perspectives recorded India’s proposal for a USD 1 trillion annual climate-finance goal, while the 2025 COP30 analysis described the agreed goals of USD 300 billion annually from developed countries and USD 1.3 trillion collectively by 2035. [4][6]
- Recommendations included blended finance, de-risking investments, and stronger public-private partnerships to help address the finance gap. [4]

### Adaptation and equitable access
- Discussions called for stronger support for adaptation, which was described as underfunded compared with mitigation; proposals included directing some proceeds from Article 6.4 mechanisms toward adaptation. [1][5]
- Participants highlighted the need for accessible funding, stronger local and institutional capacity, and simpler ways to obtain finance through multilateral institutions. [4]
- Equity principles, including common but differentiated responsibilities, were identified as important to finance negotiations and to how responsibilities and support are shared. [1][4][6]

reply.question: How does TERI support climate-smart agriculture and improve soil productivity?
reply.answer:
TERI supports climate-smart agriculture through research and practical solutions that aim to make farming more climate-resilient and resource-efficient while improving soil health and crop productivity [1][5]. Its work includes nature-based and biological inputs, advanced agricultural technologies, and ways to reuse agricultural waste [1][4][8].

### Farming practices and support
- TERI’s strategy includes enabling farmers to adopt climate-smart and regenerative practices, including nanofertilizers, and using nature-based solutions to improve soil health [5].
- It develops solutions to reduce dependence on synthetic chemical inputs while improving nutrient-use efficiency, carbon sequestration and crop productivity [1].
- TERI supports farmers through field demonstrations, need-based technologies and agricultural knowledge; earlier work in Uttarakhand also aimed to strengthen farmer livelihoods and local food security [6].

### Soil health and productivity
- TERI’s mycorrhizal biofertilizers are designed to improve nutrient uptake, soil structure and soil health, while supporting plant growth and more efficient use of water and nutrients [8].
- In field trials reported for 2015–16, mycorrhiza fortified with nitrogen-fixing bacteria was tested with pea, kidney bean and millet in Uttarakhand; reported yield increases were 30% for kidney bean and 25% each for millet and pea [6].
- TERI’s three biologically produced nanofertilizers—nano-Urea, nano-DAP and nano-Phosphorus—were reported to reduce demand for chemical nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizers by 25–50% and increase yields by 8–25% across different crops and agro-ecological zones [7].
- In trials reported in the 2023–24 annual-report edition, TERI’s mycorrhizal biofertilizer Superrhiza could substitute approximately 20–25% of recommended chemical-fertilizer doses; the report says it was used on about one million acres between April 2023 and March 2024 [8].

### Agricultural waste and other research
- TERI researches turning agricultural waste into soil amendments and nutrient solutions. Work with IOCL and ICAR-IARI used lignin-rich digestate from biorefineries to improve soil fertility, microbial activity and input-use efficiency [4].
- Its wider agricultural research includes microbial products, soil-microbiome engineering, tissue-culture plants, nanofertilizers and nanopesticides, and technologies for allied areas such as livestock feed and pest management [1][8].

### Glazing and façade design
- The window-to-wall ratio (WWR) matters: one study in Shillong found maximum energy savings at 30% WWR, with savings falling significantly as glazed area increased [1]. - Glazing properties—including U-value, solar heat gain coefficient (SHGC) and visible light transmittance (VLT)—affect heat flow, solar gains and daylight. Selection involves balancing heat control with useful daylight; low-E coatings and double glazing can reduce heat transfer, while lower SHGC can reduce cooling demand [2][3].
- Orientation, window size and geometry, building form, and the surrounding environment influence solar exposure, heat gain and daylight distribution. East- and west-facing façades need particular attention to shading; orientation and shading should be considered together [2][3][5].
- Frames and installation also matter: metal frames can increase overall heat gain, and infiltration losses can add to energy consumption [2][3].

### Shading, daylight and comfort
- External shading devices, such as projections, can control solar heat and glare; the sources describe external shading as more effective than internal shading [2][3].
- Daylight can reduce electric-lighting use, but excessive glazing or poorly controlled glare can undermine that benefit. Daylight-linked controls can coordinate natural and artificial lighting [2][3].
- Glazing and shading choices affect both energy use and visual comfort. In the Shillong study, proposed combinations were assessed for energy consumption, daylight availability and glare across different façade orientations [1].

### Building systems and conditions
- Façade performance interacts with HVAC and lighting systems. Careful HVAC selection and sizing, appropriate control settings, and coordination with glazing and shading help meet cooling demand efficiently [3].
- Internal heat gains from people and equipment also influence cooling needs; in buildings with high internal loads, the article advises addressing heat build-up inside as well as the façade [2][3].
